MUJAHID:v2p762#2/r1.author: Mujāhid b. Jabr
MUJAHID:v2p762#2/r1.speaker: مجاهد
MUJAHID:v2p762#2/r1.claim: Mujahid says the moon follows the sun.

FARRA:v3p266/r2.author: al-Farrāʾ
FARRA:v3p266/r2.speaker: author
FARRA:v3p266/r2.claim: The kasra in rhyming forms from wāw roots follows the yāʾ-based pattern begun in the sūra; a sequence beginning in wāw could instead take fatḥa throughout.

FARRA:v3p266/r3.author: al-Farrāʾ
FARRA:v3p266/r3.speaker: author
FARRA:v3p266/r3.claim: Ḥamza's opening of wāw-derived forms while keeping kasra on yāʾ forms shows poor grasp of Arabic patterns; with wāw alone he prefers fatḥa, while yāʾ permits either vowel.

FARRA:v3p266/r4.author: al-Farrāʾ
FARRA:v3p266/r4.speaker: author
FARRA:v3p266/r4.claim: The moon follows the sun and takes some of its light; following and coming after are equivalent in Arabic.

ABDURRAZZAQ:v3p376/r1.author: ʿAbd al-Razzāq al-Ṣanʿānī
ABDURRAZZAQ:v3p376/r1.speaker: قتادة
ABDURRAZZAQ:v3p376/r1.claim: Qatada says the moon follows the sun on the night of the new crescent.

TAB-FULL:v24p436/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v24p436/r1.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v24p436/r1.claim: The moon follows the sun during the first half of the month, rising after the sun sets.

TAB-FULL:v24p436/r2.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v24p436/r2.speaker: ابن عباس، مجاهد، قتادة
TAB-FULL:v24p436/r2.claim: The reported explanations say the moon follows the day or sun, especially when the new crescent appears after sunset.

TAB-FULL:v24p436/r3.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v24p436/r3.speaker: ابن زيد
TAB-FULL:v24p436/r3.claim: Ibn Zayd describes the full cycle: the moon follows the sun in the first half of the month, then leads it in the second half.

ZAJJAJ:v5p331#2/r1.author: al-Zajjāj
ZAJJAJ:v5p331#2/r1.speaker: author
ZAJJAJ:v5p331#2/r1.claim: The moon follows the sun “when” it follows; another explanation is that the moon becomes full and follows the sun in brightness and light.

IBNABIHATIM:v10p3436/r1.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v10p3436/r1.speaker: ابن عباس
IBNABIHATIM:v10p3436/r1.claim: Ibn Abbas says the moon follows the sun.

IBNABIHATIM:v10p3437/r12.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v10p3437/r12.speaker: قتادة
IBNABIHATIM:v10p3437/r12.claim: Qatadah identifies the sun with daytime, the moon as following the new moon at its setting, and daylight as covering the sun.

IBNABIHATIM:v10p3437/r2.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v10p3437/r2.speaker: مجاهد
IBNABIHATIM:v10p3437/r2.claim: Mujahid says the moon follows the sun.

NAHHAS:v5p235/r2.author: Abū Jaʿfar al-Naḥḥās
NAHHAS:v5p235/r2.speaker: author
NAHHAS:v5p235/r2.claim: The ordinary meaning of talāhā is that the moon follows the sun; al-Farrāʾ reports that the moon takes its light from it.

FARISI-HUJJA:v6p418/r1.author: Abū ʿAlī al-Fārisī
FARISI-HUJJA:v6p418/r1.speaker: ابن كثير وعاصم وابن عامر
FARISI-HUJJA:v6p418/r1.claim: Ibn Kathīr, ʿĀṣim, and Ibn ʿĀmir open the endings in this sūrah, al-Layl, and al-Ḍuḥā.

FARISI-HUJJA:v6p418/r2.author: Abū ʿAlī al-Fārisī
FARISI-HUJJA:v6p418/r2.speaker: الكسائي
FARISI-HUJJA:v6p418/r2.claim: Al-Kisāʾī uses imālah throughout these endings and the endings of al-Layl and al-Ḍuḥā.

FARISI-HUJJA:v6p418/r3.author: Abū ʿAlī al-Fārisī
FARISI-HUJJA:v6p418/r3.speaker: حمزة
FARISI-HUJJA:v6p418/r3.claim: Ḥamzah varies the endings: he inclines ḍuḥāhā but opens talāhā and ṭaḥāhā, while inclining the remaining forms, including sajā and daḥāhā.

FARISI-HUJJA:v6p418/r4.author: Abū ʿAlī al-Fārisī
FARISI-HUJJA:v6p418/r4.speaker: نافع
FARISI-HUJJA:v6p418/r4.claim: Nāfiʿ has several transmissions: some make the endings intermediate, while Warsh and Qālūn are also reported to open them all; another report opens only talāhā and inclines the rest.

FARISI-HUJJA:v6p418/r5.author: Abū ʿAlī al-Fārisī
FARISI-HUJJA:v6p418/r5.speaker: أبو عمرو
FARISI-HUJJA:v6p418/r5.claim: Abū ʿAmr is reported as using intermediate imālah, while ʿAbbās reports fully inclined forms for selected endings; other transmissions describe his treatment across verse endings.

FARISI-HUJJA:v6p418/r6.author: Abū ʿAlī al-Fārisī
FARISI-HUJJA:v6p418/r6.speaker: author
FARISI-HUJJA:v6p418/r6.claim: Imālah is licensed where the alif behaves as one originating in yāʾ, as in derived verbs and nouns; an alif from wāw, such as العصا, normally resists it.

FARISI-HUJJA:v6p418/r7.author: Abū ʿAlī al-Fārisī
FARISI-HUJJA:v6p418/r7.speaker: author
FARISI-HUJJA:v6p418/r7.claim: Rare inclined examples with an alif from wāw are too uncommon to challenge the general pattern.

THALABI:v10p212#3/r4.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v10p212#3/r4.speaker: author
THALABI:v10p212#3/r4.claim: The moon follows the sun, taking its light and rising after it sets during the first half of the month.

MAWARDI-FULL:v6p281#2/r10.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v6p281#2/r10.speaker: الطبري
MAWARDI-FULL:v6p281#2/r10.claim: Al-Tabari locates it on the fifteenth, when the moon rises with sunset.

MAWARDI-FULL:v6p281#2/r11.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v6p281#2/r11.speaker: ابن زيد
MAWARDI-FULL:v6p281#2/r11.claim: Ibn Zayd says the moon follows through the month, with their apparent order reversing between its halves.

MAWARDI-FULL:v6p281#2/r12.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v6p281#2/r12.speaker: author
MAWARDI-FULL:v6p281#2/r12.claim: Mawardi also suggests the moon is behind the sun at night, each governing its own time: sun by day and moon by night.

MAWARDI-FULL:v6p281#2/r7.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v6p281#2/r7.speaker: مجاهد
MAWARDI-FULL:v6p281#2/r7.claim: Mujahid says the moon follows the sun by matching it.

MAWARDI-FULL:v6p281#2/r8.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v6p281#2/r8.speaker: ابن عباس
MAWARDI-FULL:v6p281#2/r8.claim: Ibn Abbas says the moon follows the sun.

MAWARDI-FULL:v6p281#2/r9.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v6p281#2/r9.speaker: قتادة
MAWARDI-FULL:v6p281#2/r9.claim: Qatada locates this following on the month's first night, when the moon is seen as the sun sets.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v24p50#2/r1.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v24p50#2/r1.speaker: المفسرون
WAHIDI-BASIT:v24p50#2/r1.claim: Talaha means followed it; layth says talā yatlū is to follow, and al-Kisaʾi gives two forms for the verbal noun.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v24p50#2/r2.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v24p50#2/r2.speaker: عطاء عن ابن عباس
WAHIDI-BASIT:v24p50#2/r2.claim: The moon's following means its appearance after the sun has set.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v24p50#2/r3.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v24p50#2/r3.speaker: المفسرون
WAHIDI-BASIT:v24p50#2/r3.claim: In the first half of the month, the moon follows the setting sun in brightness and succeeds it in light.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v24p50#2/r4.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v24p50#2/r4.speaker: قتادة والكلبي
WAHIDI-BASIT:v24p50#2/r4.claim: They place the following on the crescent night: after sunset, the new moon appears and follows it below the horizon.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v24p50#2/r5.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v24p50#2/r5.speaker: الفراء
WAHIDI-BASIT:v24p50#2/r5.claim: He says the moon follows by taking its light from the sun, just as following someone's word means taking it up; a cited poem says the moon gains its light from her.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v24p50#2/r6.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v24p50#2/r6.speaker: الزجاج
WAHIDI-BASIT:v24p50#2/r6.claim: He says the moon follows when it becomes full and follows the sun in brightness on the white nights.

WAHIDI-QT:91:2/r1.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-QT:91:2/r1.speaker: author
WAHIDI-QT:91:2/r1.claim: The moon follows the sun in light during the month's first half, taking over its light.

WAHIDI-WAJIZ:91:1-8/r2.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:91:1-8/r2.speaker: author
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:91:1-8/r2.claim: During the first half of the month the moon follows the sun in light and replaces it.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p435#2/r2.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p435#2/r2.speaker: author
BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p435#2/r2.claim: The moon follows the sun during the month’s first half: after sunset it follows its illumination; al-Zajjaj says this is its full phase during the bright nights.

KASHSHAF:91:2/r1.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF:91:2/r1.speaker: author
KASHSHAF:91:2/r1.claim: The moon follows the sun by rising as it sets and taking its light, during the first half of the month.

KASHSHAF:91:2/r2.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF:91:2/r2.speaker: author
KASHSHAF:91:2/r2.claim: Alternatively, when the moon becomes full it follows the sun in brightness and light.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v4p762/r2.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v4p762/r2.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v4p762/r2.claim: The moon follows the sun by rising as the sun sets and taking its light during the first half of the month; alternatively, it follows when full in brightness.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v4p762/r5.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v4p762/r5.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v4p762/r5.claim: The repeated wāws can govern both accusative and genitive: the oath-wāw omits its verb altogether and substitutes for it, while coordinated wāws inherit that double function, resolving the apparent two-governor problem.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p487#2/r10.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p487#2/r10.speaker: قتادة
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p487#2/r10.claim: Qatada specifically locates this following on the full-moon night, when the sun sets as the moon rises.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p487#2/r6.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p487#2/r6.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p487#2/r6.claim: The moon follows the sun around the new moon through midmonth in their setting, then follows it in the reverse arrangement during the latter half.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p487#2/r7.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p487#2/r7.speaker: الحسن بن أبي الحسن
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p487#2/r7.claim: Al-Hasan says the moon follows the sun continually because it draws its light from it; Ibn Atiyya says this is not limited to either half of the month.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p487#2/r8.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p487#2/r8.speaker: الفراء
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p487#2/r8.claim: Al-Farra also interprets following as continual dependence on the sun.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p487#2/r9.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p487#2/r9.speaker: الزجاج وغيره
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p487#2/r9.claim: Al-Zajjaj and others say the moon becomes full and round, following the sun in rank, brightness, and magnitude.

TABRISI:91:1-15/r5.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:91:1-15/r5.speaker: author
TABRISI:91:1-15/r5.claim: The moon follows the sun by taking light from it and succeeding it in the sky.

TABRISI:91:1-15/r6.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:91:1-15/r6.speaker: الحسن
TABRISI:91:1-15/r6.claim: The moon follows the sun on the first night of the month, appearing as the sun sets.

TABRISI:91:1-15/r7.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:91:1-15/r7.speaker: author
TABRISI:91:1-15/r7.claim: Other timings are the fifteenth night or the whole month, with the moon preceding the sun in the first half and following its setting in the second.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p137#2/r1.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p137#2/r1.speaker: ابن عباس
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p137#2/r1.claim: One interpretation is that the moon follows the sun; several timings are offered for this following.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p137#2/r2.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p137#2/r2.speaker: قتادة
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p137#2/r2.claim: On the first night of the month, the moon follows when it becomes visible after sunset.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p137#2/r3.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p137#2/r3.speaker: الماوردي
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p137#2/r3.claim: On the fifteenth, the moon follows as it rises with sunset.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p137#2/r4.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p137#2/r4.speaker: علي بن أحمد النيسابوري
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p137#2/r4.claim: During the month's first half, the moon follows the sun after sunset in brightness and trails it in light.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p137#2/r5.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p137#2/r5.speaker: مجاهد
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p137#2/r5.claim: Alternatively, the moon follows the sun by matching it in brightness when full, during the white nights.

RAZI:91:2/r1.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI:91:2/r1.speaker: الليث
RAZI:91:2/r1.claim: Layth glosses تلا يتلو as following something.

RAZI:91:2/r2.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI:91:2/r2.speaker: عطاء عن ابن عباس
RAZI:91:2/r2.claim: One view says the moon follows the sun’s light by remaining visible after sunset during the first half of the month.

RAZI:91:2/r3.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI:91:2/r3.speaker: قتادة والكلبي
RAZI:91:2/r3.claim: Qatada and al-Kalbi say the moon follows the sun in setting on the night of the new crescent.

RAZI:91:2/r4.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI:91:2/r4.speaker: الفراء
RAZI:91:2/r4.claim: Al-Farraʾ takes following to mean receiving light from the sun, as one person follows another by taking from him.

RAZI:91:2/r5.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI:91:2/r5.speaker: الزجاج
RAZI:91:2/r5.claim: Al-Zajjaj says the moon follows the sun when it becomes rounded and full, matching the sun in brightness during the white nights.

RAZI:91:2/r6.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI:91:2/r6.speaker: author
RAZI:91:2/r6.claim: Another view sees the moon as following in apparent size and in how its motion affects worldly interests; astronomy shows a special relation between moon and sun.

RAZI-FULL:v31p171/r1.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v31p171/r1.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v31p171/r1.claim: The sura urges obedience and warns against disobedience; oaths by beneficial created things prompt reflection and gratitude because divine oaths weigh heavily on the heart.

RAZI-FULL:v31p171/r5.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v31p171/r5.speaker: الفراء
RAZI-FULL:v31p171/r5.claim: Al-Farra explains imala in endings with roots from waw by their resemblance to words beginning with ya; forms such as tala and daha can shift toward ya in verbs.

RAZI-FULL:v31p171/r6.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v31p171/r6.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v31p171/r6.claim: Full non-imala is also sound because many Arabs do not incline these alifs toward ya, and letters that historically shifted from waw or ya do not always reveal the shift in pronunciation.

RAZI-FULL:v31p171/r7.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v31p171/r7.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v31p171/r7.claim: Hamza's mixed approach is also good: only alifs derived from ya warrant imala, while tala, daha and similar forms derive from waw.

RAZI-FULL:v31p172/r10.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v31p172/r10.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v31p172/r10.claim: A further view says the moon follows in apparent size and its relation to worldly interests, with a special astronomical affinity to the sun.

RAZI-FULL:v31p172/r6.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v31p172/r6.speaker: عطاء عن ابن عباس
RAZI-FULL:v31p172/r6.claim: The moon follows the sun by remaining visible after its setting in the first half of the lunar month.

RAZI-FULL:v31p172/r7.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v31p172/r7.speaker: قتادة والكلبي
RAZI-FULL:v31p172/r7.claim: Qatada and al-Kalbi say the moon follows the sun by setting after it on the new moon night.

RAZI-FULL:v31p172/r8.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v31p172/r8.speaker: الفراء
RAZI-FULL:v31p172/r8.claim: Al-Farra understands following as taking light from the sun.

RAZI-FULL:v31p172/r9.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v31p172/r9.speaker: الزجاج
RAZI-FULL:v31p172/r9.claim: Al-Zajjaj says the moon follows the sun when it becomes full and nearly matches its brightness on the white nights.

RAZI-FULL:v31p173#2/r2.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v31p173#2/r2.speaker: القفال
RAZI-FULL:v31p173#2/r2.claim: Al-Qaffal says all four oaths are really about the sun through its midday light, the moon's borrowing its light, its emergence in daytime and its concealment at night.

QURTUBI-FULL:91:2/r1.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:91:2/r1.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:91:2/r1.claim: The moon follows the sun when it becomes visible after sunset; talaw means to follow.

QURTUBI-FULL:91:2/r2.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:91:2/r2.speaker: قتادة
QURTUBI-FULL:91:2/r2.claim: He says this occurs on the night of the new moon, when the moon is seen after sunset.

QURTUBI-FULL:91:2/r3.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:91:2/r3.speaker: ابن زيد
QURTUBI-FULL:91:2/r3.claim: In the first half of the month the moon follows the setting sun by rising afterward; in the second half it follows by setting after it.

QURTUBI-FULL:91:2/r4.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:91:2/r4.speaker: الفراء
QURTUBI-FULL:91:2/r4.claim: He says the moon takes some of the sun's light.

QURTUBI-FULL:91:2/r5.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:91:2/r5.speaker: الزجاج
QURTUBI-FULL:91:2/r5.claim: Another view says the moon resembles the sun in light and brightness when full and round.

BAYDAWI-FULL:91:1-4/r2.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:91:1-4/r2.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:91:1-4/r2.claim: The moon follows the sun’s rising early in the month, its setting at full moon, or the sun’s cycle of form and light.

NASAFI-FULL:v4p341#5/r1.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v4p341#5/r1.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v4p341#5/r1.claim: The moon follows the sun in brightness and light during the first half of the month, taking over its light.

QASHANI:91:1-3/r2.author: ʿAbd al-Razzāq al-Qāshānī
QASHANI:91:1-3/r2.speaker: author
QASHANI:91:1-3/r2.claim: The moon is the heart, which follows the spirit into illumination and turns toward it; following the ego would eclipse it.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p484/r7.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p484/r7.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p484/r7.claim: The Meccan surah swears by parts of the upper and lower worlds and by the soul as an instrument of reflection; it moves from disbelievers' afterlife to their worldly destruction and eventual Fire.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p485/r10.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p485/r10.speaker: الزجاج وغيره
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p485/r10.claim: Al-Zajjāj and others gloss the phrase as becoming full and round; the moon follows the sun in light and magnitude as no other planet does.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p485/r11.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p485/r11.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p485/r11.claim: One account says that in the month's second half the sun sets as the moon rises, while in the first half the moon sets after the sun.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p485/r12.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p485/r12.speaker: الزمخشري
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p485/r12.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī says the moon rises at sunset, drawing on the sun's light during the first half of the month.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p485/r6.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p485/r6.speaker: الحسن والفراء
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p485/r6.claim: Al-Hasan and al-Farrāʾ say the moon habitually follows the sun because it receives its light from it.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p485/r7.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p485/r7.speaker: ابن زيد
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p485/r7.claim: Ibn Zayd says the moon follows the sun throughout the month, rising after it in the first half and setting after it in the second.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p485/r8.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p485/r8.speaker: ابن سلام
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p485/r8.claim: Ibn Sallām limits the following to the first half: the moon takes the sun's place and rises after it sets.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p485/r9.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p485/r9.speaker: قتادة
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p485/r9.claim: Qatada takes the referent to be the full moon: the sun sets and the moon rises.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p486/r3.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p486/r3.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p486/r3.claim: For eloquence, all the pronouns through يغشاها should refer to the sun; this matches the preceding description of day revealing it.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p486/r5.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p486/r5.speaker: القفال
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p486/r5.claim: Al-Qaffāl summarizes the oaths as four solar aspects: daytime brightness and activity, the moon taking its light, full appearance, and disappearance at night.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p487/r1.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p487/r1.speaker: أصحابنا
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p487/r1.claim: The author's colleagues interpret سبحان من سخركن as a proper name, with mā infinitival and temporal.

SAMIN-DURR:91:2-3#2/r1.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:91:2-3#2/r1.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:91:2-3#2/r1.claim: The Shaykh invokes the Sibawayh poem as a case of coordinating a genitive plus nominative pair with another pair; the author says this concedes the disputed coordination, though the poem has an additional complication.

SAMIN-DURR:91:2-3#2/r2.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:91:2-3#2/r2.speaker: الخليل
SAMIN-DURR:91:2-3#2/r2.claim: Al-Khalil says the last two wāws in the oath sequence coordinate nouns, while the first is like the prepositional wāw and the tā’ of swearing.

SAMIN-DURR:91:2-3#2/r3.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:91:2-3#2/r3.speaker: ابن كيسان
SAMIN-DURR:91:2-3#2/r3.claim: Ibn Kaysan permits an explicit oath verb with the wāw, as in ‘I swear by God that Zayd is standing’; the author says this objection does not bind al-Zamakhshari’s position.

SAMIN-DURR:91:2-3#2/r4.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:91:2-3#2/r4.speaker: الشيخ
SAMIN-DURR:91:2-3#2/r4.claim: The Shaykh identifies the deeper puzzle as finding a governor for a future ‘idha’ after an oath: the present oath verb, an implied event, the oath object itself, and an implied circumstantial all face objections.

SAMIN-DURR:91:2-3#3/r1.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:91:2-3#3/r1.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:91:2-3#3/r1.claim: The Shaykh’s preference that conjunction does not itself govern does not compel al-Zamakhshari, who chooses the alternative grammatical doctrine.

SAMIN-DURR:91:2-3#3/r2.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:91:2-3#3/r2.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:91:2-3#3/r2.claim: The author insists that the construction does involve two governors: oath wāw governs the genitive and the oath verb governs the time adverb, with both sets of complements coordinated.

SAMIN-DURR:91:2-3#3/r3.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:91:2-3#3/r3.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:91:2-3#3/r3.claim: The Sibawayh poem cited by the Shaykh acknowledges coordination across the two governors, even though the Shaykh relies on Sibawayh’s authority.

SAMIN-DURR:91:2-3#3/r4.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:91:2-3#3/r4.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:91:2-3#3/r4.claim: Mentioning Ibn Kaysan’s permission to state an oath verb does not refute al-Zamakhshari, because the latter need not share Ibn Kaysan’s view.

SAMIN-DURR:91:2-3#3/r5.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:91:2-3#3/r5.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:91:2-3#3/r5.claim: The Shaykh’s example with a second time phrase preceding the coordinated noun does parallel the verse’s governors, though it raises a separate issue of repeating the construction.

SAMIN-DURR:91:2-3#3/r6.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:91:2-3#3/r6.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:91:2-3#3/r6.claim: Al-Khalil’s description as ‘disfavored’ supports prohibition rather than rebutting al-Zamakhshari; the Shaykh has either softened the term or misunderstood it.

SAMIN-DURR:91:2-3#3/r7.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:91:2-3#3/r7.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:91:2-3#3/r7.claim: An omitted construct such as ‘rising of the star’ can be the governor; the author says an oath now may refer to an object that will exist later, so the tense mismatch is no objection.

SAMIN-DURR:91:2-3#3/r8.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:91:2-3#3/r8.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:91:2-3#3/r8.claim: A deleted governor before ‘idha’ is possible as a prospective circumstantial; the oath verb still governs it, and the circumstantial may be understood prospectively.

SAMIN-DURR:91:2-3#3/r9.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:91:2-3#3/r9.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:91:2-3#3/r9.claim: If the sworn object is a physical entity, one can supply an event, making the temporal phrase a circumstantial attached to that event; Ibn al-Hajib addressed the question and the author notes extended debate.

SAMIN-DURR:91:2-3/r2.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:91:2-3/r2.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:91:2-3/r2.claim: The ‘idha’ clauses raise a syntactic problem: a conditional needs an answer, while a purely temporal phrase needs a governor; the oath verb is present-time and cannot straightforwardly govern a future time phrase.

SAMIN-DURR:91:2-3/r3.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:91:2-3/r3.speaker: الزمخشري
SAMIN-DURR:91:2-3/r3.claim: Al-Zamakhshari answers that an oath wāw suppresses its verb and stands for both the verb and preposition; following coordinating wāws can therefore govern the same accusative and genitive pattern.

SAMIN-DURR:91:2-3/r4.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:91:2-3/r4.speaker: الشيخ
SAMIN-DURR:91:2-3/r4.claim: The Shaykh rejects the claim that a conjunction governs by standing in for a governor; he says the governor of the coordinated element is the same as for its antecedent, though he does not insist on that point against al-Zamakhshari.

SAMIN-DURR:91:2-3/r5.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:91:2-3/r5.speaker: الشيخ
SAMIN-DURR:91:2-3/r5.claim: The Shaykh says the verse coordinates two nouns with matching case roles, rather than coordinating across two governors, and offers ‘passing by Zayd standing and ‘Amr sitting’ as the pattern.

SAMIN-DURR:91:2-3/r6.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:91:2-3/r6.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:91:2-3/r6.claim: The Shaykh cites a line in Sibawayh that coordinates a genitive and a nominative with another genitive and nominative as a parallel construction.

IBNKATHIR:91:2/r3.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR:91:2/r3.speaker: قتادة
IBNKATHIR:91:2/r3.claim: The moon follows on the night of the new moon, when it is seen after sunset.

IBNKATHIR:91:2/r4.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR:91:2/r4.speaker: ابن زيد
IBNKATHIR:91:2/r4.claim: In the first half of the month the moon follows the sun, and in the second half the sun follows the moon.

IBNKATHIR:91:2/r5.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR:91:2/r5.speaker: مالك عن زيد بن أسلم
IBNKATHIR:91:2/r5.claim: Alternatively, it means the moon follows the sun on the Night of Decree.

BIQAI-FULL:v8p437#2/r5.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v8p437#2/r5.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v8p437#2/r5.claim: The moon follows the sun by reflecting its light: proximity dims it, distance increases its illuminated portion to the full moon, then nearness again makes it wane; ‘following’ is a metaphor.

DURR-FULL:v8p527/r10.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v8p527/r10.speaker: ابن عباس عن عكرمة
DURR-FULL:v8p527/r10.claim: He glossed the moon as following the sun.

DURR-FULL:v8p527/r8.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v8p527/r8.speaker: ابن عباس
DURR-FULL:v8p527/r8.claim: He glossed the sun as its light, the moon as following it, daylight as illuminating it, God as builder of heaven, the earth as spread out, inspiration as showing good and evil, and corruption as leading astray.

DURR-FULL:v8p527/r9.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v8p527/r9.speaker: ابن عباس
DURR-FULL:v8p527/r9.claim: In another report the moon follows the day, what the earth contains is what God created in it, and inspiration teaches obedience and disobedience.

BURSEVI:v10p340#3/r3.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v10p340#3/r3.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v10p340#3/r3.claim: The moon follows the sun after its setting, drawing on the sun's light during the month's first half; al-Raghib says following can mean bodily succession, imitation, or following in judgment, recitation, and reflection.

BURSEVI:v10p340#3/r4.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v10p340#3/r4.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v10p340#3/r4.claim: The moon receives its light from the sun and is like its deputy; radiance ranks above light, since every radiance is light but not every light is radiance.

BURSEVI:v10p340#3/r5.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v10p340#3/r5.speaker: شيخي وسندي
BURSEVI:v10p340#3/r5.claim: The cited spiritual master says the sun is a sign of the all-comprehensive and most perfect divine reality.

BURSEVI:v10p340#3/r6.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v10p340#3/r6.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v10p340#3/r6.claim: In the inward reading, the moon is the heart following the spirit, turning toward it and receiving its light rather than following the ego into darkness.

BURSEVI:v10p341#2/r1.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v10p341#2/r1.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v10p341#2/r1.claim: Although the conditional sense of idha seems to require an answer and an operator, the author reads it causally in these oaths: swear because the moon follows, the day reveals, and the night covers; al-Qamus also allows a present-time meaning, “when.”

BURSEVI:v10p341#2/r7.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v10p341#2/r7.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v10p341#2/r7.claim: The oath wa's are conjunctive and share the implied verb, avoiding the problem of coordinating words governed by different agents or multiplying oaths with one answer.

ALUSI-FULL:v30p140#2/r1.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v30p140#2/r1.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v30p140#2/r1.claim: “Following” can mean the moon rises after the sun early in the month; the moon is then like the young morning, and the crescent becomes visible after sunset.

ALUSI-FULL:v30p140#2/r2.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v30p140#2/r2.speaker: قتادة
ALUSI-FULL:v30p140#2/r2.claim: Qatada's view is that the moon follows the sun's setting at full moon on the fourteenth night, rising at the eastern horizon opposite the setting sun; the moon is then at its full strength.

ALUSI-FULL:v30p140#2/r3.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v30p140#2/r3.speaker: ابن زيد
ALUSI-FULL:v30p140#2/r3.claim: Ibn Zayd says the moon follows the sun throughout the lunar month: by rising during the first half and by setting during the second.

ALUSI-FULL:v30p140#2/r4.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v30p140#2/r4.speaker: ابن سلام
ALUSI-FULL:v30p140#2/r4.claim: Ibn Sallam says the moon follows the sun by receiving and displaying light from it during the waxing half; al-Zamakhshari prefers this explanation.

ALUSI-FULL:v30p140#2/r5.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v30p140#2/r5.speaker: الحسن والفراء
ALUSI-FULL:v30p140#2/r5.claim: Al-Hasan and al-Farra say the moon follows the sun at all times because its illumination comes from the sun; Alusi says the changing phases and loss of light when Earth blocks sunlight make this clear.

ALUSI-FULL:v30p140#2/r6.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v30p140#2/r6.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v30p140#2/r6.claim: Alusi disputes the claim that early authorities never held lunar light to derive from sunlight; alternative explanations for the phases or disappearance during Earth's obstruction are weaker.

ALUSI-FULL:v30p140#2/r7.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v30p140#2/r7.speaker: الزجاج
ALUSI-FULL:v30p140#2/r7.claim: Al-Zajjaj and others say tala can mean to fill out and become round, so the moon follows the sun in rounding and reaching full light.

ELMALILI:91:2/r1.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:91:2/r1.speaker: author
ELMALILI:91:2/r1.claim: The moon follows the sun most fully when it rises after sunset as a bright full moon, especially on nights fourteen to sixteen.

ELMALILI:91:2/r10.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:91:2/r10.speaker: author
ELMALILI:91:2/r10.claim: The crescent-night interpretation draws attention to the new moon, but restricting following to sunset alone lacks a decisive reason.

ELMALILI:91:2/r11.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:91:2/r11.speaker: author
ELMALILI:91:2/r11.claim: The first view illuminates the moon's day-by-day waxing toward fullness more broadly than the fourth view.

ELMALILI:91:2/r12.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:91:2/r12.speaker: author
ELMALILI:91:2/r12.claim: Ultimately, the fourth view is clearest: the full moon resembles a secondary sun and its reflected light prepares for the soul's perfection.

ELMALILI:91:2/r13.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:91:2/r13.speaker: author
ELMALILI:91:2/r13.claim: The moon's reflected, nonfiery light leads from sensory evidence to intelligible truth, the seen to the unseen, and effect to its cause.

ELMALILI:91:2/r14.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:91:2/r14.speaker: author
ELMALILI:91:2/r14.claim: Reading talā figuratively likens the moon's spreading the unseen sun's reflected light to a reciter explaining a Qur'anic verse; this evokes the purified soul and the Qur'an as light.

ELMALILI:91:2/r2.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:91:2/r2.speaker: author
ELMALILI:91:2/r2.claim: The moon can seem to follow the sun at other times, but before fullness it is incomplete and after the sixteenth night it increasingly lags behind sunset.

ELMALILI:91:2/r3.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:91:2/r3.speaker: author
ELMALILI:91:2/r3.claim: The verb talā derives from tulūw, meaning to follow behind; recitation is related because a reader follows and conveys words.

ELMALILI:91:2/r4.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:91:2/r4.speaker: Atâ
ELMALILI:91:2/r4.claim: Atā, transmitting from Ibn ʿAbbās, says the moon remains risen when the sun sets, which occurs in the first half of the month.

ELMALILI:91:2/r5.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:91:2/r5.speaker: Katâde ile Kelbî
ELMALILI:91:2/r5.claim: Qatada and Kalbi say the moon follows the sun by setting after it, as on the crescent night.

ELMALILI:91:2/r6.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:91:2/r6.speaker: Ferrâ
ELMALILI:91:2/r6.claim: Farra interprets following as the moon receiving its light from the sun.

ELMALILI:91:2/r7.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:91:2/r7.speaker: Zeccâc
ELMALILI:91:2/r7.claim: Zajjaj takes the phrase as the moon's turning and completion, when its light reaches fullness and it resembles the sun in illumination.

ELMALILI:91:2/r8.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:91:2/r8.speaker: author
ELMALILI:91:2/r8.claim: A fifth possibility relates the moon's perceptible size and the world's benefits to its movement.

ELMALILI:91:2/r9.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:91:2/r9.speaker: author
ELMALILI:91:2/r9.claim: The reported senses share the idea of following or resembling the sun in rising, setting, light, size, or benefit; the moon also derives its light from the sun.

QUTB-ZILAL:91:2/r1.author: Sayyid Quṭb
QUTB-ZILAL:91:2/r1.speaker: author
QUTB-ZILAL:91:2/r1.claim: The moon follows the sun with its gentle, clear, delicate light and awakens an ancient, deep bond in the human heart, inspiring quiet praise and spiritual renewal.

IBNASHUR:91:2/r1.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR:91:2/r1.speaker: author
IBNASHUR:91:2/r1.claim: Tala means following: moonlight follows sunlight after sunset, figuratively, and the moon follows the sun through its phases; at the full moon its following is literal around sunset.

IBNASHUR:91:2/r2.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR:91:2/r2.speaker: author
IBNASHUR:91:2/r2.claim: The crescent appears after sunset for three nights; near its first visibility and at full moon it follows the sun, and it illuminates many nights as a substitute for sunlight.

IBNASHUR:91:2/r3.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR:91:2/r3.speaker: author
IBNASHUR:91:2/r3.claim: The restriction to the moon's following highlights its visible manifestation, making the oath one by the moon and by the time it follows the sun, like the duha oath.

IBNASHUR:91:2/r4.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR:91:2/r4.speaker: author
IBNASHUR:91:2/r4.claim: The verse signals that moonlight is borrowed from sunlight striking the moon's earth-facing surface, rather than being intrinsic; Ibn Ashur calls this a scientific miracle noted in his tenth introduction.

IBNASHUR:91:2/r5.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR:91:2/r5.speaker: author
IBNASHUR:91:2/r5.claim: The order symbolizes Islam: the sun's guidance leaves no path for error and promises worldwide spread, while the moon shining in darkness resembles Islam's first appearance amid polytheism.

IBNASHUR:91:2/r6.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR:91:2/r6.speaker: author
IBNASHUR:91:2/r6.claim: Day and night then represent Islam's clarity after polytheist error, opposite the order in Surat al-Layl; sky, earth, and finally the human soul follow as signs of guidance and misguidance.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p366/r1.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p366/r1.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p366/r1.claim: The oath confirms the threat of destruction implicitly conveyed by the news; each waw following a pause is an oath particle, and the sun, moon, sky, earth, and human soul display God's wise and powerful creation.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p366/r2.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p366/r2.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p366/r2.claim: The dawn brightness, moon following the sun, daylight, and night are all examples of the fine order God established.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p366/r5.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p366/r5.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p366/r5.claim: Following means the moon's light appearing after sunset, figuratively following the sun; its phases also follow the sun, and at full moon it literally appears around sunset. Its illumination replaces the sun for several nights, so the oath highlights its visible following state as well as the moon itself.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p368/r2.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p368/r2.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p368/r2.claim: إذا is a circumstantial time adverb attached to the state of each moon, day, and night; each is sworn by in the condition that best displays God's artistry.

TABATABAI:91:1-8/r3.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:91:1-8/r3.speaker: author
TABATABAI:91:1-8/r3.claim: The moon follows the sun either by deriving its light from it, a constant state, or by rising after sunset, from crescent to fullness.

ASAD-NOTES:91:1#n1/r1.author: Muhammad Asad
ASAD-NOTES:91:1#n1/r1.speaker: Al-Farra
ASAD-NOTES:91:1#n1/r1.claim: Al-Farra says the moon follows the sun by deriving its light from it.

ASAD-NOTES:91:1#n1/r2.author: Muhammad Asad
ASAD-NOTES:91:1#n1/r2.speaker: Raghib
ASAD-NOTES:91:1#n1/r2.claim: Raghib gives the same interpretation of the moon's following the sun.

CORPUSCORANICUM:91:1-8:anmerkung/r1.author: Nicolai Sinai (Frühmekkanische Suren), with Nora K. Schmid, using preparatory work by Angelika Neuwirth; later parts Dirk Hartwig, Angelika Neuwirth et al. (author line per sura in segments)
CORPUSCORANICUM:91:1-8:anmerkung/r1.speaker: author
CORPUSCORANICUM:91:1-8:anmerkung/r1.claim: Qur'anic oaths probably draw on a characteristic expression of pre-Islamic soothsayers, though the connection remains insufficiently researched.

CORPUSCORANICUM:91:1-8:anmerkung/r2.author: Nicolai Sinai (Frühmekkanische Suren), with Nora K. Schmid, using preparatory work by Angelika Neuwirth; later parts Dirk Hartwig, Angelika Neuwirth et al. (author line per sura in segments)
CORPUSCORANICUM:91:1-8:anmerkung/r2.speaker: author
CORPUSCORANICUM:91:1-8:anmerkung/r2.claim: The structure and function of cumulative oath series are discussed at 93:1–2, with many parallels.

CORPUSCORANICUM:91:1-8:kommentar/r1.author: Nicolai Sinai (Frühmekkanische Suren), with Nora K. Schmid, using preparatory work by Angelika Neuwirth; later parts Dirk Hartwig, Angelika Neuwirth et al. (author line per sura in segments)
CORPUSCORANICUM:91:1-8:kommentar/r1.speaker: author
CORPUSCORANICUM:91:1-8:kommentar/r1.claim: An eight-verse oath series leads into the antithetical statement in verses 9–10; the pre-Islamic genre is repurposed in verses 5–7 to express biblical creation ideas.

CORPUSCORANICUM:91:1-8:kommentar/r2.author: Nicolai Sinai (Frühmekkanische Suren), with Nora K. Schmid, using preparatory work by Angelika Neuwirth; later parts Dirk Hartwig, Angelika Neuwirth et al. (author line per sura in segments)
CORPUSCORANICUM:91:1-8:kommentar/r2.speaker: author
CORPUSCORANICUM:91:1-8:kommentar/r2.claim: The series moves through three complementary or contrasting pairs—sun/moon, night/day, heaven/earth—then the soul, whose opposed moral capacities are specified in verse 8.

CORPUSCORANICUM:91:1-8:kommentar/r4.author: Nicolai Sinai (Frühmekkanische Suren), with Nora K. Schmid, using preparatory work by Angelika Neuwirth; later parts Dirk Hartwig, Angelika Neuwirth et al. (author line per sura in segments)
CORPUSCORANICUM:91:1-8:kommentar/r4.speaker: author
CORPUSCORANICUM:91:1-8:kommentar/r4.claim: The oath series narrows from cosmic creation, traced vertically from celestial bodies to earth, to the human moral subject.

CORPUSCORANICUM:91:1-8:kommentar/r5.author: Nicolai Sinai (Frühmekkanische Suren), with Nora K. Schmid, using preparatory work by Angelika Neuwirth; later parts Dirk Hartwig, Angelika Neuwirth et al. (author line per sura in segments)
CORPUSCORANICUM:91:1-8:kommentar/r5.speaker: author
CORPUSCORANICUM:91:1-8:kommentar/r5.claim: Its shift from creation to humanity resembles the 81:1–14 sequence, which evokes the world's eschatological dissolution rather than cyclical operation.

CORPUSCORANICUM:91:1-8:kommentar/r6.author: Nicolai Sinai (Frühmekkanische Suren), with Nora K. Schmid, using preparatory work by Angelika Neuwirth; later parts Dirk Hartwig, Angelika Neuwirth et al. (author line per sura in segments)
CORPUSCORANICUM:91:1-8:kommentar/r6.speaker: author
CORPUSCORANICUM:91:1-8:kommentar/r6.claim: A caesura after verse 4 divides effects and activities of the oath's objects in verses 1–4 from references to God's creating activity in verses 5–8.

CORPUSCORANICUM:91:1:anmerkung/r2.author: Nicolai Sinai (Frühmekkanische Suren), with Nora K. Schmid, using preparatory work by Angelika Neuwirth; later parts Dirk Hartwig, Angelika Neuwirth et al. (author line per sura in segments)
CORPUSCORANICUM:91:1:anmerkung/r2.speaker: author
CORPUSCORANICUM:91:1:anmerkung/r2.claim: The translation signals paired oaths by beginning verses 2, 4, and 6 with and, following Neuwirth.

CORPUSCORANICUM:91:2:anmerkung/r1.author: Nicolai Sinai (Frühmekkanische Suren), with Nora K. Schmid, using preparatory work by Angelika Neuwirth; later parts Dirk Hartwig, Angelika Neuwirth et al. (author line per sura in segments)
CORPUSCORANICUM:91:2:anmerkung/r1.speaker: author
CORPUSCORANICUM:91:2:anmerkung/r1.claim: The moon oath parallels references to the moon in 84:18 and 74:32.

CORPUSCORANICUM:91:2:anmerkung/r2.author: Nicolai Sinai (Frühmekkanische Suren), with Nora K. Schmid, using preparatory work by Angelika Neuwirth; later parts Dirk Hartwig, Angelika Neuwirth et al. (author line per sura in segments)
CORPUSCORANICUM:91:2:anmerkung/r2.speaker: author
CORPUSCORANICUM:91:2:anmerkung/r2.claim: One might translate talā as the moon falling behind the sun, but the parallel between verses 1–3 and 2–4 favors the moon's following the day into night.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p329/r2.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p329/r2.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p329/r2.claim: The world appears to contain opposing forces, yet God keeps them within limits and in harmony; their accord preserves the universe.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p331/r1.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p331/r1.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p331/r1.claim: The sun, moon, day, and night are complementary phenomena; their apparent oppositions in appearance, temperament, and effects serve in harmony.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p331/r2.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p331/r2.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p331/r2.claim: Earlier sūrahs used this complementarity for arguments about monotheism and the Day of Judgement; here the focus is how the apparent opposites work together.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p332/r1.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p332/r1.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p332/r1.claim: The cosmic order prevents the sun or moon from intruding on the other’s appointed time and keeps day and night within their roles, as 36:40 says.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p332/r2.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p332/r2.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p332/r2.claim: Harmony among opposites sustains the universe; their obedience to limits teaches people to stay within God’s bounds, since exceeding them creates disorder God will not tolerate.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p335/r6.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p335/r6.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p335/r6.claim: Some take 91:9–10 as the oath’s complement; Islahi gives weight to al-Zamakhsharī’s rejection of that view.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p335/r7.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p335/r7.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p335/r7.claim: The sun, moon, day, and night show that a powerful, self-sustaining God keeps the world’s elements on their appointed paths, preventing their collision from destroying it.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p336/r3.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p336/r3.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p336/r3.claim: Suppressing the complement lets everything evident from the oaths count as its content; one prominent implication is that God destroys rebellious nations.

KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:91:1/r1.author: Hayreddin Karaman, Mustafa Çağrıcı, İbrahim Kâfi Dönmez, Sadrettin Gümüş
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:91:1/r1.speaker: author
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:91:1/r1.claim: Oaths by natural phenomena highlight cosmic order and its benefits, the Creator's power, and the importance of what follows.

KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:91:1/r3.author: Hayreddin Karaman, Mustafa Çağrıcı, İbrahim Kâfi Dönmez, Sadrettin Gümüş
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:91:1/r3.speaker: author
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:91:1/r3.claim: The moon following the sun may mean its light follows or derives from the sun, moonlight rises after sunset, or the moon is in its first crescent phase.

STUDYQURAN:91:2/r1.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:91:2/r1.speaker: some
STUDYQURAN:91:2/r1.claim: Some read the moon following the sun as an allusion to the moon receiving sunlight.

STUDYQURAN:91:2/r2.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:91:2/r2.speaker: others
STUDYQURAN:91:2/r2.claim: Others see the new crescent at the start of each lunar month, appearing near sunset and setting soon after.

STUDYQURAN:91:2/r3.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:91:2/r3.speaker: some
STUDYQURAN:91:2/r3.claim: Another reading alludes to the different orbits of sun and moon as measures of time.
